text: One Sabbath, when Jesus went to eat at the house of a leading Pharisee, they were watching him closely.
And there in front of him was a man whose body was badly swollen.

versions.text: And there in front of him was a man suffering from dropsy.
versions.explanation: "Dropsy" is an archaic medical term that most listeners will not understand when the text is read aloud. Rendering ὑδρωπικός descriptively ("whose body was badly swollen") keeps the sense and reads naturally; a footnote such as "Greek: suffering from dropsy, an abnormal accumulation of fluid" could preserve the technical term.

text: Jesus spoke up and asked the experts in the law and the Pharisees, "Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath or not?"
But they said nothing. So he took hold of the man, healed him, and sent him on his way.
Then he said to them, "If one of you has a son or an ox that falls into a well, will you not pull him out at once, even on the Sabbath day?"
And they could give no answer to this.
Noticing how the guests were choosing the places of honor, he told them this parable:
"When you are invited to a wedding feast, do not take the place of honor, for someone more distinguished than you may have been invited.
Then the host who invited you both will come and say to you, 'Give this man your place,' and you will be humiliated as you move to the lowest place.

Instead, when you are invited, go and take the lowest place, so that when your host comes he will say to you, 'Friend, move up to a better place.' Then you will be honored in front of all the other guests.
For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and the one who humbles himself will be exalted."

Then he said to his host, "When you give a lunch or a dinner, do not invite your friends, your brothers, your relatives, or your rich neighbors. If you do, they may invite you in return, and you will be repaid.
Instead, when you give a banquet, invite the poor, the crippled, the lame, the blind.
Then you will be blessed, because they cannot repay you. You will be repaid at the resurrection of the righteous."
When one of those at the table heard this, he said to him, "Blessed is the one who will eat bread in the kingdom of God."
Jesus replied, "A man was giving a great banquet, and he invited many guests.
At the hour of the dinner he sent his servant to tell those who had been invited, 'Come, everything is ready now.'
But one after another they all began to make excuses. The first said, 'I have bought a field, and I must go and see it. Please excuse me.'
Another said, 'I have bought five pairs of oxen, and I am on my way to try them out. Please excuse me.'
Still another said, 'I have just gotten married, so I cannot come.'

The servant came back and reported this to his master. Then the master of the house became angry and said to his servant, 'Go out quickly into the streets and alleys of the town and bring in the poor, the crippled, the blind, and the lame.'
'Sir,' the servant said, 'what you ordered has been done, and there is still room.'
Then the master said to the servant, 'Go out to the roads and the country lanes and make them come in, so that my house may be full.
For I tell you, not one of those men who were invited will taste my dinner.'"

versions.text: For I tell you, not one of those men who were invited will taste my banquet.'"
versions.explanation: "Taste my banquet" is an awkward collocation in English. Since δεῖπνον is rendered "dinner" in verse 17, using "dinner" here also keeps the parable's vocabulary consistent and reads more smoothly aloud.

text: Large crowds were traveling with him, and he turned and said to them:
"If anyone comes to me and does not hate his father and mother, his wife and children, his brothers and sisters—yes, even his own life—he cannot be my disciple.
Whoever does not carry his own cross and follow me cannot be my disciple.
Suppose one of you wants to build a tower. Will he not first sit down and count the cost, to see whether he has enough to finish it?
Otherwise, if he lays the foundation and is unable to complete it, everyone who sees it will begin to mock him,
saying, 'This man began to build and could not finish.'
Or suppose a king is setting out to engage another king in war. Will he not first sit down and consider whether with ten thousand men he can stand against the one coming at him with twenty thousand?
And if he cannot, he will send a delegation while the other is still far off and ask for terms of peace.
In the same way, any one of you who does not give up everything he has cannot be my disciple.
Salt is good, but if salt loses its taste, how can it be made salty again?
It is fit neither for the soil nor for the manure pile; it is thrown away. Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear."
